opus-5.5.text:
I think there's still a lot of room. If you look back over the past few years, almost every major jump in capability has come from finding a better way to turn more compute and data into better generalization. Pre-training on next-token prediction was the first big one: compressing the whole internet forces the model to learn something fairly general about the world. But we're starting to hit limits there. High-quality natural data is finite, and simply making the model bigger on the same distribution gives diminishing returns.

So the question becomes: where does the next increment of generalization come from? My view is that it increasingly comes from letting the model generate its own experience, through reinforcement learning, long chains of reasoning, and interaction with environments like tools, code, and the web. Once the model can explore, make mistakes, get feedback, and learn from that, you're no longer bounded by the data humans happened to write down. In a sense, data turns into a product of compute rather than a fixed input.

There are real open problems. Rewards are easy to define for math or code, where you can verify the answer, but much harder for open-ended tasks like writing, research, or judgment calls. If we can't find good signals there, generalization will be uneven: very strong in verifiable domains, weaker elsewhere. Long-context ability matters a lot too. A lot of what we call "intelligence" is the ability to hold a complex situation in mind over many steps, and that is still far from solved.

But I'm fundamentally optimistic. I don't think we've seen a ceiling. Generalization isn't one thing you either have or don't have. It's something you keep pushing by finding the right objective, the right data, and the right way to scale. Every time it looked like we'd plateaued, someone found a new axis to scale along. I expect that to keep happening, and I think the teams that do well will be the ones that identify the next axis early and commit to it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says, “I don’t think we’ve seen a ceiling,” and expects progress to continue through new axes of scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
I think generalization is really the central question, and I'm fairly optimistic about it, but with some caveats about where the gains come from.

If you look at the history of the last few years, almost every step up in generalization came from the same thing: scale plus a training objective that forces the model to compress more of the world. Next-token prediction on a huge, diverse corpus is a very good objective because to do it well you have to implicitly learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, even some world models. So the first-order answer is still scaling, and I don't think we've hit the wall there. The data wall is real, but I think it's more of a bottleneck for a particular recipe than a fundamental limit.

The more interesting part is what happens when pretraining data gets scarce. My view is that the next phase of generalization comes from reinforcement learning, where the model generates its own experience. With RL you're not limited to what humans happened to write down. The model tries things, gets a signal, and learns from the outcome. What we've seen with long chain-of-thought reasoning is a good example: the model learns to plan, verify, backtrack, and these skills transfer across math, code, and even open-ended tasks that weren't the explicit training target. That's a form of generalization that pretraining alone wasn't giving us.

The challenge is that RL generalizes well where you have a reliable reward, and reality is mostly messy. So a lot of the work now is about building good reward signals for fuzzy domains, and about making sure the model doesn't just overfit to the verifier. If you solve that, I think you get something closer to a system that can keep improving from interaction, which is a qualitatively different kind of generalization than what we had before.

So in short: scaling isn't over, the objective is shifting from imitation toward experience, and I'd bet the biggest improvements in generalization over the next few years come from how we design that experience, not just from more parameters.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling has not hit a fundamental wall and describes systems that can keep improving through interaction, suggesting there may be no final limit to generalization improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room to improve generalization. The key question is whether a model can apply what it has learned to a situation that looks quite different from its training examples. Doing well on familiar tasks is useful, but it doesn’t fully answer that question.

One direction is to improve the way models learn, rather than simply give them more examples. Can they discover underlying principles and reuse them across tasks? Another is to let them learn through interaction: try something, observe the result, and revise their approach. That could help with problems where static training data provides limited guidance.

I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t assume that every increase in scale automatically brings the kind of generalization we want. We need evaluations that distinguish familiarity from the ability to handle genuinely new problems. That will help us understand which improvements are fundamental and where we still need new ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says there is still room to improve and expresses optimism, but does not suggest that improvement may have no final limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room to improve generalization. The key question is whether a model has learned an underlying principle or simply learned patterns that happen to work well on familiar tasks. Those can look very similar until you put the model in a new situation.

One direction is to give models more diverse problems where the same underlying idea appears in different forms. Another is to let them interact with an environment, try things, and learn from feedback. That gives them opportunities to discover consequences rather than only predict what someone else would say.

But we also need better ways to measure progress. If we keep optimizing against a fixed set of benchmarks, it becomes difficult to distinguish broader capability from adaptation to those benchmarks. I’m optimistic about continued improvement, but I’d judge it by how reliably a model handles unfamiliar problems, especially when the assumptions change.

r001.rationale: The response says there is still room for improvement and expresses optimism about continued improvement, but it does not suggest that improvement has no final limit.
